About this item

  • IN THE BOX: 20-pack of 1.5 volt AA alkaline batteries for reliable performance across a wide range of devices
  • DEVICE COMPATIBLE: Ideal battery for game controllers, toys, flashlights, digital cameras, clocks, and more
  • DESIGNED TO LAST: 10-year leak-free shelf life; store for emergencies or use right away
  • EASY USE & STORAGE: Ships in Certified Frustration-Free Packaging; easy to open and store extras for later use
  • SINGLE USE: These batteries are NOT rechargeable; for rechargeable options, check out Amazon Basics rechargeable batteries
  • For frequent/professional/industrial use, check out Amazon Basics Industrial AA batteries.

How customer reviews and ratings work

Customer Reviews, including Product Star Ratings help customers to learn more about the product and decide whether it is the right product for them.

To calculate the overall star rating and percentage breakdown by star, we don’t use a simple average. Instead, our system considers things like how recent a review is and if the reviewer bought the item on Amazon. It also analyzed reviews to verify trustworthiness.

Customers say

Good batteries have been using for years without issue at great price
Amazon Basics AA Alkaline Batteries, 48 Count I use these Amazon Basics AA alkaline batteries because, in the grim little battlefield of household electricity, they deliver a very respectable price-to-performance ratio. Do they outperform every heavily advertised copper-topped or bunny-powered celebrity battery in every possible device under every condition known to man, beast, monkey, Tasmanian devil, and suspiciously blinking smoke detector? I cannot swear that before Congress. But in my actual real-world use, they perform well, last a reasonable amount of time, and cost less than the brands with marketing budgets large enough to be seen from orbit. The box contains 48 batteries, arranged as four 12-packs, which is a civilized way to package them. It lets you store them without having one giant loose herd of AA batteries rolling around in a drawer like tiny metallic livestock. I use AA batteries in remotes, clocks, flashlights, small electronics, wireless keyboards, mice, toys, meters, and all the other little devices that quietly drain civilization one alkaline cell at a time. These Amazon Basics batteries have been reliable for that kind of use. They seem to have a useful life comparable to the major brands, although battery life is one of those subjects where everyone becomes a laboratory scientist after changing two batteries in a TV remote. Unless you are doing controlled discharge testing under identical load, temperature, humidity, and device conditions, most of us are operating on educated suspicion and household folklore. Formula 1: Battery Value = Useful Life ÷ Price Per Cell By that formula, these do very well. They may not arrive wearing a tuxedo and waving a national advertising campaign, but they get the job done. Formula 2: Household Sanity = Number of Spare Batteries ÷ Number of Devices Screaming “Low Battery” A 48-pack improves household sanity. Not completely, because nothing can fully protect us from the 2 a.m. chirping smoke detector, that demon flute of domestic despair, but it helps. Now, because I am apparently unable to review a battery without dragging the entire periodic table into the courtroom, let us discuss what an alkaline battery actually is. A typical alkaline AA battery is basically a small sealed chemical factory. It uses zinc at the anode, manganese dioxide at the cathode, and potassium hydroxide as the alkaline electrolyte. The casing is steel, the separator keeps the internal materials from shorting directly, the current collector helps move electrons, and the label gives it the modest dignity of appearing like a consumer product rather than a tiny controlled corrosion tube. Formula 3: Chemical Energy → Electrical Energy + Heat + Inevitable Drawer Clutter The basic alkaline battery reaction involves zinc being oxidized and manganese dioxide being reduced. In simplified form: Zn + 2MnO2 + H2O → ZnO + 2MnOOH There are more detailed half-reactions, because chemistry enjoys making simple things wear a doctoral robe: Anode reaction: Zn + 2OH⁻ → ZnO + H2O + 2e⁻ Cathode reaction: 2MnO2 + 2H2O + 2e⁻ → 2MnOOH + 2OH⁻ The electrons then go off to perform their tiny assigned labor, powering your remote control so you can watch television instead of confronting the yawning philosophical emptiness of modern life. Formula 4: Remote Control Function = Electron Flow × Button Presses ÷ Human Laziness And yes, the potassium hydroxide inside is corrosive. That is why alkaline batteries can leak if old, damaged, badly stored, or left too long in a device. A leak is not battery juice in the fun sense. It is caustic chemical misery creeping into your flashlight like a white crusty ghost of poor planning. Store them properly, do not mix old and new batteries, do not mix brands or chemistries in the same device, and remove them from devices you are not using for long periods. Formula 5: Leak Risk = Age + Heat + Neglect + Bad Storage Habits As for manufacturing, these batteries are usually private-label products, and the actual factory source may vary by batch. Amazon Basics AA alkalines have been commonly associated with FDK / Fujitsu-related manufacturing and reported Indonesian production, but that is batch-dependent. I am not going to pretend I personally toured the factory wearing a clipboard and a moral superiority helmet. Still, it is fair to say battery manufacturing, wherever it occurs, is an industrial process with real environmental consequences. There is mining. There is refining. There is zinc. There is manganese dioxide. There is steel. There is electrolyte. There is plastic packaging. There are paperboard boxes. There is shipping. There are containers. There are trucks. There are forklifts. There are freighters crossing oceans with the quiet menace of global commerce. Somewhere, a container full of batteries may be stacked next to plastic flamingos, discount patio lights, and a pallet of products destined to fail in nine months. Such is the poetry of civilization. Formula 6: Consumer Convenience = Industrial Complexity Hidden From View We push a button. The TV changes channels. But behind that miracle is mining, chemical processing, factory labor, packaging, maritime shipping, warehousing, last-mile delivery, and eventually disposal. That does not make these bad batteries. It makes them modern batteries. I do worry about the environmental side of disposable batteries in general. Alkaline batteries are safer and less toxic than some older battery types, and many places allow normal disposal, but they are still not environmental fairy dust. Multiply one AA battery by millions of households and suddenly you are not talking about a junk drawer. You are talking about a waste stream with little metal cylinders flowing through it like a consumer-age river. Formula 7: Waste Stream Burden = Number of Batteries Used × Frequency of Replacement × Human Indifference And yes, plastic packaging matters too. These come in a box with four packs of 12, which is relatively practical, but packaging is still packaging. There is paperboard, wrapping, labeling, ink, adhesive, and all the small material decisions that eventually become part of the landfill economy. The container world is another rabbit hole. Batteries may travel by sea freight, and sea freight brings its own industrial theater: fuel consumption, emissions, shipping lanes, port congestion, bridge strikes, and the faint possibility of a freighter carrying consumer goods smacking into infrastructure while humanity stands around saying, “Well, that seems expensive.” To be absolutely clear, I am not saying this box of batteries is going to knock down a bridge. I am saying modern supply chains have become so vast and strange that your television remote may have a more complicated journey than your ancestors did crossing a continent. Now, let us discuss Indonesia, pollution, and the uncomfortable underside of inexpensive goods. I do not know where this exact box was made unless confirmed by the packaging, and I am not making a specific claim about this batch. But battery production in general involves mining, chemical processing, metal forming, electrolyte handling, and waste management. If pollution control is weak in any manufacturing region, the burden can fall on workers, water systems, soil, and surrounding communities. It is not romantic. It is not clean. It is not the cheerful little “10-year shelf life” line on the package. It is chemistry, labor, and regulation. The uncomfortable formula: Low Retail Price = Efficient Manufacturing + Scale + Supply Chain Pressure + Costs Someone Else May Absorb That last part is the one we prefer not to think about while searching for the remote. And factory workers? Again, I cannot say anything about any specific facility involved in this product. But globally, industrial workers in chemical and metal-processing industries can face exposure risks if safety systems, ventilation, training, protective equipment, and enforcement are inadequate. The fact that our flashlight works during a power outage should not make us completely forget the human infrastructure behind it. Now, tsetse flies. Do these batteries directly affect tsetse flies? Not unless someone is trying to power a very tiny insect disco in sub-Saharan Africa, and even then I have questions. But the global industrial system that produces disposable goods affects habitats, transport patterns, waste, emissions, and ecosystems in broad ways. Tsetse flies, monkeys in Africa, sea birds, Tasmanian devils, and every other creature unlucky enough to share a planet with our packaging habits exist in the downstream consequences of human production. The batteries are not personally hunting tsetse flies. They are not cackling in a lab coat. But no product is completely isolated from the system that made it. And speaking of batteries, I do miss film cameras. There was a time when AA batteries powered simple cameras, flashes, and little motor drives, and you could drop film off at a Fotomat kiosk. Remember Fotomat? Those little huts in parking lots where film went in and, through some alchemy of chemicals and patience, photographs came back? Now everyone has 42,000 digital photos on a phone, six of them worth keeping, and no one prints anything unless a grandparent threatens legal action. Progress has given us convenience, but it has also stolen the strange delight of waiting to find out whether your vacation photos were good or whether you spent nine dollars developing 24 blurry images of someone’s thumb. In actual use, these batteries are boring in the best possible way. They work. They are reasonably priced. They store well. They fit devices properly. They are available in a useful quantity. They are not rechargeable, so if you use batteries heavily in high-drain devices, rechargeable batteries may make more economic and environmental sense. But for remotes, clocks, emergency flashlights, occasional-use gadgets, and general household battery reserves, these are a solid buy. Formula 8: Best Use Case = Low-to-Moderate Drain Devices + Bulk Storage + Reasonable Price For high-drain devices, rechargeables often make more sense: Rechargeable Advantage = Reuse Cycles × Reduced Waste ÷ Upfront Cost But disposable alkaline batteries still have a role. They store well. They are simple. They are ready when needed. They do not require a charger. They are good for emergency bins, remotes, clocks, and devices where slow, steady power is the mission. The 75-point good, bad, and ugly summary: 1. These are AA alkaline batteries. 2. The package includes 48 batteries. 3. They are arranged as four packs of 12. 4. That packaging layout is convenient. 5. They are easy to store. 6. The price is one of the biggest advantages. 7. The performance is good for the money. 8. They work well in common household devices. 9. They are suitable for remote controls. 10. They are suitable for clocks. 11. They are suitable for flashlights. 12. They are suitable for wireless mice. 13. They are suitable for wireless keyboards. 14. They are suitable for toys. 15. They are suitable for small electronics. 16. They seem to last about as well as major advertised brands in ordinary use. 17. I cannot prove that without laboratory testing. 18. Household battery impressions are often anecdotal. 19. Still, my real-world use has been positive. 20. They provide good value. 21. They do not feel like bargain-bin junk. 22. They are not rechargeable. 23. That is clearly stated. 24. For frequent use, rechargeables may be better. 25. For occasional use, alkalines are still convenient. 26. They have a claimed long shelf life. 27. Long shelf life is useful for emergency storage. 28. They are good to keep in a drawer. 29. They are good to keep with flashlights. 30. They are good to keep with storm supplies. 31. They are good for devices that sit unused for periods of time. 32. They should still be stored properly. 33. Heat is bad for batteries. 34. Moisture is bad for batteries. 35. Mixing old and new batteries is a bad habit. 36. Mixing battery brands in the same device is also not ideal. 37. Leaving batteries in unused devices for years is asking for leakage. 38. Alkaline leakage can damage devices. 39. Potassium hydroxide is corrosive. 40. Battery leaks are not charming. 41. The chemistry is well-established. 42. Zinc and manganese dioxide do the useful work. 43. The steel casing gives structure. 44. The separator prevents internal chaos. 45. The electrolyte allows ion movement. 46. The label makes the tiny chemical tube look friendly. 47. These batteries are simple to use. 48. No charger is needed. 49. No app is needed. 50. No firmware update is needed, mercifully. 51. They just go into the device and work. 52. That is increasingly rare in modern life. 53. The branding is plain. 54. The packaging is practical. 55. The value proposition is strong. 56. They compete well against famous brands. 57. Heavily advertised batteries may not always justify the higher price. 58. These are especially good when bought in quantity. 59. The environmental downside is real. 60. Disposable batteries add to the waste stream. 61. Manufacturing batteries requires metals and chemicals. 62. Mining and refining have environmental impacts. 63. Shipping has environmental impacts. 64. Packaging has environmental impacts. 65. Industrial production is not magically clean. 66. The low price reflects scale and supply chain efficiency. 67. It may also reflect the hidden costs of global manufacturing. 68. I cannot verify the exact factory for this box. 69. The likely manufacturing background may vary by batch. 70. Battery production should be taken seriously from a worker-safety standpoint. 71. These batteries are not responsible for every ecological disaster on Earth. 72. They are also not guilt-free objects descended from the heavens. 73. They are practical, useful, and imperfect. 74. I will continue using them because they perform well for the price. 75. Overall, they are a favorable buy, provided you use them intelligently and dispose of them responsibly. Final verdict: Amazon Basics AA alkaline batteries are a strong value. They perform well in normal household devices, cost less than many heavily advertised brands, and come in a useful 48-count package that makes sense for storage and regular use. They are not rechargeable, they are not environmentally innocent, and they do carry the usual disposable-battery concerns about manufacturing, materials, leakage, and waste. But as practical AA batteries for everyday use, they do the job well. They power the remote. They keep the clocks alive. They sit in the drawer until called upon. They may not have the glamorous advertising mythology of the famous brands, but in my devices, they have worked reliably. And in a world without Fotomat kiosks, film cameras in every glovebox, or any remaining dignity in the junk drawer, that is enough.

    I bought this 48-pack of Amazon Basics AA batteries for a mix of household devices—remote controls, wireless mice, kids' toys, and a digital clock. After three months of use, I’m thoroughly impressed with the performance.

    Pros:

    - Price per battery is unbeatable compared to big-name brands. You get 48 cells for what you’d normally pay for 24.

    - Longevity is solid. In a high-drain wireless mouse, they lasted about 40% longer than a store-brand economy pack I tried before.

    - Shelf life is real: I still have a sealed pack from a year ago that shows full voltage when tested.

    - No leakage so far, even in devices left on for weeks.

    Cons:

    - Not rechargeable—so for heavy-use gadgets like game controllers, you might want to rechargeables. These are best for moderate-use or backup items.

    - Packaging can be tough to open; you’ll need scissors to get the first few out.

    Overall: If you need a bulk supply of reliable, long-lasting alkaline batteries without paying a premium, this is the best deal on Amazon. I’ve recommended it to family and will buy again.

    When managing a high-density equipment load—from patrol vehicle remotes to household sensors—the cost of name-brand power can scale quickly. The Amazon Basics 48-Pack AA Alkaline Batteries is a pragmatic "stockpile" solution that prioritizes sheer quantity and cost-efficiency over extreme high-drain endurance.

    Consistent Performance Across Daily Gear

    These 1.5V alkaline cells are engineered for reliable service in everyday electronics. In real-world testing, they perform on par with standard alkaline competitors when used in clocks, TV remotes, and wireless keyboards.

    Capacity: They typically deliver around 1900mAh at low discharge rates (200mA), which is competitive for their price point.

    Compatibility: They work seamlessly in game controllers and standard flashlights, providing steady power without the rapid "voltage drop" found in lower-tier generic brands.

    Emergency Readiness and Shelf Life

    The advertised 10-year shelf life is a critical feature for emergency kits and low-use equipment.

    Leak-Resistant Design: The construction includes a triple-layer safety valve to help prevent leaks, making them safer for long-term storage inside expensive equipment like digital cameras or portable radios.

    Bulk Packaging: The frustration-free cardboard box makes it easy to keep the remaining 47 batteries organized on a workshop shelf without them rolling loose in a drawer.

    The "High-Drain" Reality

    While these are excellent for most tasks, they have limitations in professional-grade high-drain scenarios.

    Intensive Use: In high-power devices like RC cars or professional camera flashes, they may only last about 80% as long as premium lithium or specialized industrial cells.

    Environmental Impact: As single-use cells, they lack the long-term sustainability and cost-per-use benefits of NiMH rechargeables for high-rotation items like Xbox controllers.

    Final Verdict

    The Amazon Basics 48-Pack is a definitive "best bang for your buck" utility. It removes the stress of running out of power for standard household and professional accessories. While they might not be the top choice for extreme high-draw gear, their reliability, quantity, and 10-year shelf life make them a fundamental staple for any organized bench or supply closet.
